query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Refining the microstructure of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 into an ultrafine-grained state promotes the rapid formation of a dense, continuous duplex oxide scale (an outer Cr2O3 layer over an inner Al2O3 layer) that limits oxygen ingress and metal cation diffusion. In the baseline (coarser-grained) condition, slower oxide formation leads to the development of brittle, non-uniform spinel oxides that crack, accelerate internal oxidation, and trigger catastrophic failure during prolonged elevated-temperature exposure under oxidizing or reducing gases.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix exhibiting a relatively coarse grain structure.
generation.intervention: Implement an ultrafine-grained processing route (e.g., via rapid solidification adjustments or post-build severe plastic deformation) to increase the density of grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (approximately 850–1050 °C) in oxidizing (or alternating oxidizing/reducing) gas environments for extended periods.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain-boundary density that accelerates diffusion pathways, allowing rapid formation of a protective duplex oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine-grained structure provides short-circuit diffusion paths for both oxygen and reactive metallic species. This accelerates the formation of a thin, adherent Cr2O3 layer on the surface followed by an inner Al2O3 layer, which together serve as an effective barrier against further oxidation. In contrast, coarser grains lead to slower and heterogeneous scale formation with the nucleation of brittle spinel phases that easily spall under thermal stress, eventually causing catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ultrafine-grained alloy will exhibit a significantly thinner and more uniform oxide scale with a clear duplex structure, reduced oxide spallation, and delayed degradation compared to the baseline coarse-grained alloy. In failure tests, the refined sample should resist catastrophic oxidation-induced cracking and internal oxidation over prolonged exposures.
generation.baseline: The as-additively manufactured alloy with a coarser grain structure forms a thick, porous, and non-uniform oxide scale (dominated by brittle spinel species) that is prone to cracking and spallation under high-temperature oxidative or reducing conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted behavior applies for exposures at elevated temperatures around 850–1050 °C under oxidizing or reducing atmospheres. Deviations outside this temperature range or different gas chemistries might not exhibit the same protective oxide evolution.
generation.uncertainty: While past evidence supports improved oxidation resistance with ultrafine-grained structures in similar HEAs, the exact kinetics of oxide layer formation and the degree of catastrophic failure prevention in this specific alloy composition under dual gas environments remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the standard additively manufactured alloy (baseline coarse grain) and another set processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure. Subject both sets to identical elevated-temperature exposures (e.g., 900 °C) in controlled oxidizing and/or reducing gaseous environments over a fixed duration (e.g., 120 h). Compare the oxide scale morphology, thickness, adhesion (via cross-sectional SEM/EDS and XRD analysis), and assess mechanical integrity under thermal cycling to identify spallation or catastrophic failure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM/EDS mapping)
Adhesion tests of the oxide scale (e.g., scratch or thermal cycling tests)
Weight gain measurements as an index of oxidation rate
Mechanical integrity assessment (presence of cracks or spallation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale thickness, improved uniformity, enhanced adhesion, and delayed onset of catastrophic failure relative to the baseline samples under the same conditions, then the hypothesis that microstructural refinement governs the protective oxide formation and governs degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. cited_evidence.text: Figure 2 shows the cross-sectional microstructure of the oxide scale formed on the Innovation Alloy, together with the high-magnification interfacial details. To clarify the effects of alloying and laser-cladding-induced nanocrystallization on oxide-scale evolution, the cross-sectional morphologies of the three alloys after oxidation at 900 °C for 120 h were compared. As shown in Figure 2a, the Base Alloy develops a thick, porous, and multilayered oxide scale with a total thickness of approximately 15.2 μm (marked by arrows), indicating rapid oxidation and limited protective capability. In contrast, the Synergy Alloy forms a much thinner and more continuous scale (approximately 1.8 μm, Figure 2b), demonstrating the beneficial role of Cr, Co, and Mn in improving scale compactness. The most compact and thinnest oxide structure is observed for the Innovation Alloy (Figure 2c), which exhibits a dense and adherent scale with a thickness of only 450 nm. cited_evidence.text: Figures 8–10 show the cross section BSE images of the oxidized samples along with their EDS elemental mapping. The elemental distribution indicates the formation of the mixed oxides in the as-cast sample oxidized at elevated temperatures, 850, 950, and 1050 °C, due to the slow diffusion of elements through GBs owing to the low number of GBs. Ultrafine grain size promotes the diffusion phenomenon owing to the higher number of GBs, which offer adequate diffusion paths for the mobility of ionic species. As-cast sample oxidized at 850 °C exhibits an oxide layer comprising Cr-, Fe-, and Co-rich oxides with a minor amount of Al2O3. However, the oxide layer formed on the surface of ultrafine-grained samples oxidized at 850 °C consists of a thin Cr2O3 layer followed by aluminum-rich inner oxides. The formation of chromia on the alloy’s surface is due to the outward diffusion of Cr ions through GBs, while alumina grows at the bottom-most oxide owing to the inward diffusion of O ions. reading.lever: Implement an ultrafine-grained processing route to rapidly form continuous, adherent protective oxide layers.
reading.why: Refining the microstructure has been demonstrated to promote cohesive oxide scale formation, which can mitigate degradation and catastrophic failure in related HEA systems.
